topic: What if time moved 10x slower, but only for you?
title: WHAT IF TIME WAS
10X SLOWER FOR YOU?

script.text: You sit down for one bite. Your pizza is already cold. You blink in class. Everyone's gone home. You tie your shoe. The sun sets.
What if time moved ten times slower, but only for you?
At first, it's amazing. A three hour car ride? Over before your song ends. Waiting for your birthday? Two days, tops.
And here's the crazy part. This is real. In nineteen-oh-five, Albert Einstein said the faster you move, the slower your time ticks. Nobody could test it. Until nineteen seventy-one.
Two scientists flew atomic clocks around the world on normal passenger planes. When they landed, the clocks were off by a few billionths of a second. Exactly what Einstein predicted.
Today, your phone depends on it. Clocks on GPS satellites run thirty-eight microseconds a day fast. That's real. Without fixing it, your map would drift ten kilometres every day.
And astronaut Scott Kelly spent a year in space. He came back about five milliseconds younger than his twin brother.
Then a man in a suit shows up. He wants to send you to space.
You say no, and go home for dinner. One hour, for you. But when you walk in, your little sister is taller than you.
Part one. Would you trade ten years for one hour? Tell me in the comments.

science.claim: GPS satellite clocks gain about 38 microseconds per day relative to ground clocks (+45 us gravity, -7 us speed).
science.working: Uncorrected, 38 us x c = ~11 km of ranging error per day.
science.source: Ashby, 'Relativity in the Global Positioning System', Living Reviews in Relativity (2003)

science.claim: Special relativity (1905) predicts moving clocks run slow.
science.source: Einstein, 'Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Korper', Annalen der Physik (1905)

science.claim: Hafele-Keating (1971): four caesium clocks flown around the world on commercial airliners differed from US Naval Observatory clocks by tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, as relativity predicts (eastward -59 ns, westward +273 ns).
Scott Kelly's year on the ISS (2015-16): he aged about 5 milliseconds less than twin Mark.
science.source: NASA Twins Study; NASA statements on time dilation
